topics: dedicated GPU sizing and burst policy
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I see Sophie, Daniel, Rachel, Omar — welcome. We're here to walk through HarborPay's requirements for Dedicated capacity and make sure Redwood's proposal lines up, so, um, quick intros please.
[00:12] Sophie (Head of ML): Hi all, Sophie here. We're exploring options to move our payment intents and fraud scoring models to a hosted/dedicated setup, mainly to reduce tail latency during checkout.
[00:20] Daniel (Platform): Daniel, I'm on infra. We manage Kubernetes on GCP today, lots of internal tooling, and we want to keep strict network controls.
[00:26] Rachel (Security): Rachel, security and compliance. I'll be validating SOC2 coverage, key management, and auditability.
[00:32] Maya (AE): Thanks. Diego from our SE team is on the call too. Diego, quick wave?
[00:36] Diego (SE): Hey everyone, hi. I'll dig into sizing and performance details.
[00:40] Maya (AE): Great. High-level are you currently running models in-house or using any hosted LLM APIs?
[00:46] Sophie: We're a mix. We run smaller, latency-critical models ourselves on prem for inference, and leverage hosted for some non-sensitive workloads. But the costs and ops burden are creeping up. We want a reserved, isolated pool with predictable unit economics and the ability to burst to extra capacity during peak events — Black Friday like spikes.
[01:05] Maya: Perfect. Can you share rough traffic patterns? QPS, token counts, concurrency?
[01:11] Sophie: Baseline is around 40 requests/sec for the payments NLP endpoints, average 150 tokens per request, with spikes up to 700 rps during promos. Most requests are short though. Latency target is p95 < 200ms for inference.
[01:23] Diego: Ok, 700 rps peaks with 150 tokens — that's useful. Are these sync requests blocking the user checkout flow?
[01:28] Sophie: Yes, for a subset of flows. Checkout validation is synchronous, so tail latency matters a lot.
[01:33] Diego: Got it. For Dedicated, we recommend a reserved pool sized for steady-state with burst capacity. There are a couple of ways — reserved GPUs with autoscale headroom or hybrid reserved plus hosted fallback. Which is your preference for data isolation?
[01:45] Daniel: We need data isolation. VPC or private deployment is preferred; we can't have raw customer data leaving our network. But we also need the ability to handle those spikes without over-provisioning full-time.
[01:57] Maya: Right — Redwood Private would give full control, but Dedicated with VPC peering and private networking can satisfy many compliance needs. Rachel, would VPC peering + zero egress to public internet meet your bar?
[02:08] Rachel: Potentially yes, but we need KMS integration and audit logs. Also, SAML/SSO and RBAC for operator access.
[02:16] Diego: We support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations in our Private offering and dedicated can be configured to use customer KMS in many setups. Audit logs and RBAC are standard for enterprise. I'll capture the exact certs.
[02:27] Sophie: You mentioned autoscale and burst. How does Redwood handle sudden spikes? We can't afford a cold-start penalty.
[02:33] Diego: We do continuous batching and a warm pool of worker processes to reduce cold starts. For Dedicated, we can keep a baseline reserved GPU count and allow burst to additional capacity — either pre-provisioned reserved burst nodes or on-demand hosted capacity as a fallback. The fallback option is faster to set up but means those tokens may transit Redwood hosted infra — not ideal if you need strict isolation.
[02:52] Daniel: The hosted fallback might be a non-starter for us. We need guaranteed isolation. Can you do elastic burst within the customer's dedicated pool?
[02:59] Diego: Yes, with Dedicated you can configure an autoscaling policy that spins up more instances in the same VPC/dedicated cluster, though capacity is constrained by region inventory. We also offer burst reservations — short-term reserved nodes that sit idle but billed differently — it's a tradeoff.
[03:14] Maya: To be explicit: we can propose a baseline of N GPUs for steady-state and M GPUs reserved for burst windows (e.g., promotions) so you avoid public fallback. Pricing reflects that.
[03:23] Sophie: Sounds reasonable. What's the expected latency on p95 with your optimized kernels and KV caching for short requests? We've seen some vendors hit 250-400ms p95 which is too high.
[03:34] Diego: For short sequences and optimized kernels we'd expect single-digit tens of ms per token; for p95 on your 150-token average, p95 under 200ms is tight but doable if you have a small model or quantized variants. Important levers are model size, batching strategy, and KV cache hit rate. Also prompt engineering to minimize tokens.
[03:51] Omar (CTO): Are you doing any model compilation or kernel selection at deploy time? We run mix of quantized and fp16 models.
[03:58] Diego: Yes, our runtime does kernel selection per model and runtime config; we support int8/4 quant and runtime optimizations. We can compile kernels tuned for your target GPU and sequence length distribution. That usually brings down latency.
[04:10] Daniel: On the networking side, we need private peering and limited egress. How do we connect? Do you support VPC peering and private link?
[04:17] Maya: We support VPC peering and private link equivalents; for Private deployments you can keep everything on-prem. For Dedicated, we typically do VPC peering and enforce strict firewall rules.
[04:26] Rachel: And what about logs and audit? We need tamper-evident logs and retention controls.
[04:31] Diego: Audit logs can be shipped to your SIEM, we support long retention and immutable stores on request. We'll include the specifics in the security pack.
[04:37] Sophie: Let's talk timeline. We want to pilot before Q1. Ideally a 1-week benchmark where you run our prompts and simulate our peaks. Can you do that?
[04:45] Maya: Absolutely — typical pilot is 1 week, we bring a benchmark harness and run it against a dedicated node pool sized for your steady-state and burst. We'll measure latency, throughput, and cost per token.
[04:55] Daniel: For the pilot, we'll need to know what sample data to provide and if any PII needs masking.
[05:01] Sophie: We'll provide anonymized prompt corpus and a traffic pattern file. We'll also note endpoints that are synchronous.
[05:07] Diego: Great. One more question — what's your current CI/CD and rollout plan for models? Do you prefer canary traffic split or blue/green?
[05:14] Sophie: We use canary rollouts and want A/B experiments. We want Redwood to support canary and automatic fallback if latency or errors rise.
[05:22] Diego: Redwood supports canaries, A/B, and automated fallback to a cheaper or smaller model if errors exceed thresholds.
[05:29] Maya: Ok let's cover costs briefly. We'll send a draft pricing table showing reserved baseline, reserved burst nodes, and estimated per-token or per-hour rates. Any budget constraints?
[05:38] Omar: We're evaluating TCO versus re-architecting our infra. We have a soft budget target but more important is predictability.
[05:44] Rachel: Also include security add-ons pricing — e.g., private network, KMS-managed keys, compliance package.
[05:50] Maya: Will do. Any competitors you're evaluating?
[05:53] Sophie: We're looking at Anthropic and Bedrock for hosted options and evaluating Cohere for some edge cases. We're pretty strict on isolation, so some hosted-only providers are lower on the list.
[06:03] Diego: Noted. For the pilot we'll need: sample prompts, peak traffic patterns, SOC requirements list, and a sample of model artifacts or model size targets.
[06:12] Sophie: We'll share those.
[06:14] Maya: Great — to summarize and capture next steps — Diego will prepare a benchmark plan and scripts; Maya will send pricing and a proposed node count and burst strategy; Rachel will list the certs and compliance items; Sophie will send prompt corpus and traffic patterns. We'll aim to kick off the pilot the week of 2026-12-14 if all goes well.
[06:36] Omar: Sounds good. One last item: are there any known limitations around cold KV cache behavior that we should expect during short-lived spikes?
[06:43] Diego: There can be warm-up effects; our runtime supports prefix caching and warm pools to mitigate, but initial ramp in a sudden spike will show higher latency. For checkout flows we typically recommend a small warm pool and pre-warm requests right before promo windows.
[06:55] Sophie: Ok. Thanks everyone. We'll reconvene after you send the docs.
[07:00] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the action items. Bye.

Notes: transcription includes minor auto-caption errors (e.g., K-V cash instead of KV cache in one snippet), occasional speaker overlap, and filler words preserved.
